item.title: Putting AI & Design Systems to work
item.content:encoded:
I just got off stage at the phenomenal Detach! Conference in Fortaleza, Brazil.

I gave my presentation using my custom eddie-slides framework, which embeds psychedelic visualizations from bf-visualzzz and showcases our course websites, my blog, and Black Friday sale webpage. I'm authoring these words using my custom content-brain editor/sharing application. And I'm not even mentioning the suite of websites I run my business with, or the new big ideas we're scheming up.

It was obvious that to teach how to use AI & Design Systems together, I'd have to walk the walk. I committed to figuring out how to get AI to consistently, reliably, and faithfully use my design system. ~18 months later, I'm so glad I did. Now, the 20+ websites I rely on to operate my business are all built and powered exclusively by our Eddie design system.

design system ↔ product connection

For as long as atomic design has been around, I've been articulating the connection between design systems and the products they serve. The design system informs & influences the products, and products inform and influence the design system.

Atomic Design Creates Connected Design Systems

Atomic design connects every layer of a design system to the real products it serves.

This vision is sound, but until recently it's been kinda hand-wavey. But I can now say I'm actually living this vision. I now have a truly system-powered product ecosystem: changes to Eddie flow into my 20+ products, and each round of product work feeds and strengthens the design system. Hooray, feedback loops!

making better products with design systems

All of our courses detail best practices for adopting design systems into your product ecosystem. Here are some free lessons from our courses demonstrating how to build with your quality design system foundations:

Generating UI With & Without The Design System

In this video, I show AI vibe-coding a UI vs AI building using the design system.

The Steel Curtain: Keeping AI Slop Out of Production

In order to not ship crap to production, I introduce the gauntlet of checks, tests, and evals that AI-written code has to pass before it ships.

Subatomic: Design Tokens at the Product Layer

Design tokens don't stop at the edge of the design system. Here's how product teams can put tokens to work in their own UI while staying connected to the system.

Also, on Wednesday we introduced skills and talked about improving your design system foundations. Now we'll highlight some skills I'm developing to improve product quality by building with your design system:

  • product-inspection: Assess your product's quality using a similar 10-station process as the design system inspection. Get humbled, but get help in improving your product quality
  • vibe-killer: (I'm really proud of this name!) converts a vibe-coded page into one built entirely from your design system
  • ds-ai-rails - an emerging skill to assess your process for keeping AI on the rails of your design system
  • product-to-storybook sucks your product's screens into your design system's Storybook to make prototyping and front-of-the-front-end work easier
  • storybook-to-product facilitates the process of translating UI you've designed in Storybook into your real product environment

These skills have helped me a ton, but they also need to be put through their paces. Give them a try, and please don't be shy about filing issues, submitting PRs, and getting in touch!

There's a lot to unpack here, but today I want to focus on a skill that I've now witnessed hundreds of people use to improve their design systems before my very eyes: /ds-inspection.

Address your design system's check engine light

Early in the creation of our AI & Design Systems course, TJ said something like "You don't want to hitch rocket boosters to the back of a car with its check engine on." In the same spirit, you don't hook AI rocket boosters up to a design system that's rickety, out of sync, and poorly documented.

That's why TJ created Figma Console MCP, FigmaLint, and a slew of other resources. That's also why we dedicate an entire chapter of our course to the myriad ways to use AI to improve the quality of your design system foundations. And that's what led me to create /ds-inspection.

The workflow I detail in the course and workshops is this:

  1. Round up all of your design system assets: codebase, design library, documentation, and other relevant resources
  2. Get Figma Console MCP up and running
  3. Run my /ds-inspection skill - answer a few questions and let 'er rip
  4. Get completely humbled by the inspection results. Most people (including me!) received a terrible first score, but good news! You also get a detailed, prioritized plan to improve it
  5. Blast through improvements to your design system, improving the quality, accessibility, parity, and AI readiness of your critical UI infrastructure

These techniques have been so helpful for improving our own system, but it's been genuinely stunning to watch a room full of people use these skills to fix and improve their respective design systems in real time. For someone who's been teaching, consulting, and guiding for over 15 years, this feels truly transformative.

Chapter 3 in AI & Design Systems details this workflow and plenty of other techniques to address your design system's check engine light. We just released 3 free video lessons from each of our courses to help you create and strengthen your design system foundations:

AI burst through the wall like the Kool-Aid Man blasting a vuvuzela, demanding everyone's attention. In fact, in this AI age those hard-earned foundations, systems, best practices, and a commitment to quality matter more than ever.

item.title: Playing My World: Helsinki Cathedral
item.content:encoded:
I'm so happy about this I could cry. For years, I've "played" my visual world: objects, architecture, cityscapes, landscapes, and anything interesting. I map the shapes and patterns I see to shapes and patterns on the fretboard. I make little compositions with those shapes and patterns.

People already think I'm weird wandering around town plunking a rubber-stringed bass ukelele, so I've I've never told anyone that I do this. It's just how my mind works. I never thought I'd be able to articulate my way of seeing/playing the world, but now I can.

So here's me "playing" the Helsinki Cathedral.

item.title: Laser Storm
item.content:encoded:
This weekend, I took Ella to her cousin's birthday party at Laser Storm on McKnight Road north of Pittsburgh. The small structure is now dwarfed by much larger, newer chain stores, but entering the doors transported me to the same amazing world my cousins and I would visit as tweens.

Behold its majesty:

Just look at these wall paintings:

Outside of the laser tag arena is the arcade area, equipped with many of the classics.

For my money, things like this need to be protected at all costs. Sure, it's a commercial enterprise, but the lack of hyper-commercialized logos, franchises, and exploitative sheen is notable. One of the signs bordering the walls says it perfectly:

"It's Not Virtual...It's REAL."

My daughter romping around with her cousins and some random kids is real. Eating bad pizza, getting sugared up, and running around playing games is real. Smoothing out dollar bills and receiving clanging tokens is real. Winning physical tickets and trading them in for penny candy and cheap-o toys is real.

This is real.

item.title: GitHub CLI: Media in issues, pull requests, and comments - GitHub Changelog
item.content:encoded:
The ability to use GitHub CLI and add Media in issues, pull requests, and comments is an absolute game-changer for people working in AI & Design Systems.

Throughout our course (and especially in Chapter 2) we talk about the fundamental shift of how git and services like GitHub are used. It is SO POWERFUL for someone on a product team to capture (manually or using tools like Playwright, which we cover in the course) and effortlessly dual-file a visual bug back into the design system repository.

I don't use game-changer that often, but historically design system teams have been fielding shit like ""This looks broken in our environment" with no additional context. So to receive a detail-rich summary AND real screenshots of the issue is genuinely a game-changer for design systems teams.

item.title: Just You Wait, by Chris Shiflett
item.content:encoded:
Just You Wait, by Chris Shiflett is a fantastic read. While I'm slightly younger than Chris, his description of the journey of growing and evolving with technology feels very familiar. The whole article is well worth a read, but really loves how he closes it out:

For the first time in years, I see possibility. Not utopia. AI’s problems aren’t being exaggerated. Like every technology before it, it will reflect the people building it. But possibility is the right word for what I’m feeling, and I haven’t felt it in a while. Not just for young people who haven’t lost their enthusiasm. For people who have been here long enough to remember when the web was open, generous, optimistic, and built by people who simply wanted to make things and share them with the world. That sharing was an expression of our gratitude, and that gratitude is still there.

I think experience matters now more than ever. I think curiosity matters. And I think a lot of people who may have quietly counted themselves out have something important to contribute.

So here’s my birthday wish, for me and for you: let’s be curious and generous. I plan to spend a lot of my time making things again. I’d love some company.

item.title: Things Take the Time They Take: A 42nd Thought at 42
item.content:encoded:
Two years ago I shared 40 thoughts as I turned 40, and last year I added a 41st thought. So as I make my 42nd lap around the sun, I figured I'd throw another thought onto the pile.

42. Things take the time they take

When I was working at R/GA, someone (I can't remember who) said something along the lines of:

You can't make a baby in one month by throwing nine people at it.

Despite this reality, I've witnessed so many cleverly attempt to hack it over the years. None have worked, and I've found the "good, fast, cheap: pick two." triangle continues to be true.

But with each passing year, time feels more compressed and our expectation of immediacy grows proportionally. The digital world introduced near-immediate abundance, which shaped our behavior, package delivery timeframes, and our willingness to wait for damn near anything. Give us another couple years and we'll all fail the fucking marshmallow test.

Creating things has become easier and more immediate as well. We now have a new paradigm of tools that allow us to generate things instantaneously. Our expectations of immediacy will shift yet again. Don't get me wrong, this convenience and immediacy can be incredible and unlock exciting new opportunities, but there are certainly costs involved.

Even though we have an arsenal of efficiency-optimizing tools and tactics at our fingertips, I've learned that when it comes to human endeavors: quality things take time the time they take.

Quality takes time to cook

Quality takes time to cook. I've learned this from putting our courses together, doing client work, writing a book, throwing a big concert, and applying myself to grand new ideas.

Through these efforts I've learned I personally can't sacrifice quality, even for things I explicitly say I'm going to cut some corners on to get out the door relatively quickly. Others might be able to dial back the quality knob to better fit the constraints of time & money, but it seems like I can't.

It's an unavoidable truth: to do big and important things takes a lot of time and energy sustained over a long period. The trick is to allow yourself to be ok with things taking the time they need to take. When I fight this statement of fact is when I get frustrated, feel guilty, feel ashamed, or feel like giving up because I'm not seeing immediate results. Complicating matters is other people's expectations of immediacy to see my results, which I still struggle with.

But for the most part, I've accepted the fact that things take the time they take. Things will get done, they will be good, and I'll do the hard work along the way to move things forward and bring ideas to life.

Front and back burner projects

In our work, I've adopted a vernacular of front burner projects and back burner projects. Our front-burner projects are the big important ones that are paying the bills and require the majority of our attention. A lot of back burner projects are the bigger ideas that can cook slowly, but you still have to occasionally stir the pot. The front burner projects eventually get done, and eventually some of those back burner projects graduate up onto the front burner.

What I've found is to allow yourself to keep stirring the pot and feel how you feel about something week over week. I've found that creating a working cadence (weekly, monthly, or otherwise) can help sustain that effort, iterate over ideas, and evolve things from idea into reality. It takes discipline to allow these things to take the time they take, but I feel like these lighter touches over longer stretches of time give things time to settle in and evolve at the necessary pace.

Valuing efforts that require time

With the rise of all this instant gratification, I hope we'll find ourselves valuing things that have clearly taken time to make. My family loves watching time lapse videos of art projects that take months and months — pencil drawings, canvases, murals, stuff that clearly requires sustained effort to arrive at a finished result. It's in the time lapse process that you can better appreciate the finished piece.

So yeah, it took me 42 years to arrive at this specific lesson, so there we go. And my advice is to just acknowledge that fact, and notice when you find yourself feeling frustrated, guilty, ashamed, or like giving up because you're not seeing immediate results in your work, your life, your relationships, and your endeavors. Things take the time they take.

item.title: Coming Up For Air
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday, I sent out a newsletter and wanted to share it here too because HOLY CRAP. It's been nearly two months since I've published a newsletter or substantive blog post, to which I say, “No sir, I don't like it.”

I'm tired of saying I'm busy (it's unhealthy, not a badge of honor), but it continues to be the truth. Just how busy, you ask? Well, I had a fantastic conversation with Don Norman (one of my all-time heroes whom I owe my career to) and literally haven't talked about it at all. Oof.

I've had to learn the hard way that there's a reason why people seclude themselves in cabins to create big projects. So while I'm still hunkered down with my big projects, my alarm clock went off so I need to come up for air, say hey, and share some big updates.

Exciting news: my website looks like crap!

If you visit bradfrost.com, you'll see that it looks like crap. Believe it or not, that's intentional.

My website has been my online home and primary means of expression for my entire adult life. We're now entering the home stretch of course production, running bi-weekly community jam sessions, and growing a helpful & supportive community. Join us!

My Atomic Design Certification Course is done!

The course contains over 10 hours of videos, sample architecture, and resources for how to master design systems: concepts, architecture, process. All backed up by a shitload of hard-earned first-hand experience. Right now, my team and I are QA-ing the included sample design system architecture in both Figma and code and putting a bow on things to get it ready for the actual launch. Consider this the last window to get the course for a comically-low price of $50 before the price increases to $150. You can also get ALL of our courses at a discount here.

SO many Wake Up Excited! episodes

  • Afyia Smith on human resiliency and docs-first design systems
  • Ridd on designers' shifting role

Whew! Keeping on theme with this update, my podcast just turned 1! Just one more thing I haven't talked about or celebrated. But for its birthday, I'd love it if you subscribe to the show on YouTube and audio!

And oh yeah, speaking of YouTube, I now have TWO YouTube channels:

  • Brad Frost - my main channel where I share ideas, design, have conversations, and more
  • Creative Exhaust - which widens my existing Cold Album Drumming project to include all of my musical and artistic shenanigans. Still very much WIP, you can watch me play music here!

Is that it???

At the beginning of this year, I declared systems bankruptcy and I've spent the entire year blowing up, overhauling, building, and bolstering all of the infrastructure and systems in my life and work. It's been difficult-yet-necessary work to do alongside getting our real projects out the door. All of this systems work is starting to bear fruit and will hopefully result in a saner, more sustainable pace moving forward. Holy shit, it better!

With this whirlwind of activity, my body, mind, and soul are looking forward to a much-needed break. Thankfully, next week I get to be a beach bum at the Outer Banks on our long-standing annual family vacation.

I hope your summer has been going well and that you've been doing interesting and restorative things! See ya soon.

item.title: Grief in the AI Age
item.content:encoded:
I want to talk about this moment in time, this AI era, through the lens of grief. Grief is a powerful response to loss. When we think about grief, we often think about death, but it's taken me a long time to understand that we grieve all sorts of non-death loss: relationships, community, home, money, dreams, expectations, identity, sense of purpose, and even the loss of ideals or ideas.

It's taken a ton of time and a hell of a lot of work to understand my own grief as I've recovered from my many and varied traumas over the years. I've also learned a ton about grief from my wife, Melissa, who through her journey to become a professional counselor has worked in hospice and other really challenging environments involving grief, death, and loss. It's through my own experience and awareness of grief that I start noticing it in other places.

AI and the 5 Stages of Grief

The explosion of AI onto the scene has caused a shock to the system has triggered a real grief response for many people —myself included. I see it in the conversations I have, and of course with the abundant opinions about it I see online.

The Five Stages of Grief, also called the Kübler-Ross model, are: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. I want to run through each one of these five stages through the lens of how you might be feeling about AI right now.

  1. Stage 1: Denial - This is certainly something that I went through, especially when AI was still generating images with seven fingers and laughable code results. It was easy to dismiss it and just push it away. I still see this with a ton of people saying, "Ha, look at how crappy it is! Look at how many mistakes it makes!" to dismiss it entirely, effectively pushing it away so as not to confront it.

  2. Stage 2: Anger - When we realize that denial isn't viable anymore, we get frustrated and start looking around to find someone to blame and take our anger out on. I feel this myself a lot, and think about this stage when I see a lot of commentary levied at the people making this technology, inflicting it on all of us with seeming reckless abandon. We get angry the many real and potential harms & risks. These feelings are certainly valid, and a lot of that anger is real and justifiable. But it's also hard because we tend to take this anger out on the people around us.

  3. Stage 3: Bargaining - Here is where we say "I'll use AI for this little thing, but not for these other bigger things. It's never going to touch my production code." Here we're trying to negotiate our complex feelings around AI; we're still angry and in denial in many respects, but we're also beginning to understand that it's here or maybe isn't entirely bad. We feel confused and are trying to make sense of it all.

  4. Stage 4: Depression - I see this a lot in many of the conversations that I have with professional designers and developers. They say something along the lines of, "What's my entire career been for if these things could just come in and generate a website in a couple seconds?" "Nothing really matters anymore. What does craft mean? What does judgment mean?" "We're all screwed; we might as well just pack it up and then go live in an underground bunker." Again, those feelings come as a natural response to pouring your heart and soul into something and feeling a real sense of loss: a loss of stability, a loss of identity, a loss of livelihood, a loss of a lot of things. That depression is real.

  5. Stage 5: Acceptance - Acceptance is really misunderstood because acceptance can be misinterpreted as, "Oh, suddenly I'm cool with all of the downsides, all of the harms, all of the risks around this technology." When someone we love dies, this acceptance stage is ultimately where we understand that person isn't coming back but you ultimately can make some form of peace with it.

    Acceptance doesn't mean that you no longer get sad or you no longer are angry that they're gone. It just means that you accept the fact that the loss has happened and that you're able to move forward with resolve. You can convert a lot of that grief into real commitment to live your life in a way that honors their memory and hopefully continues to make them proud.

Grief Is Personal and Isn't Linear

I think I went through my own stages of grief around AI a bit sooner just because my circumstances had me working with it a little earlier. I distinctly remember many conversations "Screw all this stuff, this sucks." But I'm also realizing that a lot of my grief training at a personal level has really helped me be able to navigate this moment with a better sense of clarity and understanding that I otherwise might not have had, had I not gone through a lot of that hard. Silver linings.

These five stages of grief come with a lot of caveats. Grief isn't a linear process. Every single day, we might feel depressed, angry, in denial, bargaining, or we might be in a state of acceptance. This isn't a linear step-by-step process that everyone goes through cleanly or on a uniform timeline. It's a useful tool to help us reflect on how we feel.

Striving for Acceptance & Commitment

So here's a little reflection for you with respect to your feelings about AI. Which stage of grief do you feel you're currently in: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, or acceptance?

Once again, it's important to stress that getting to acceptance doesn't mean that you're never also angry or depressed. It's just an acknowledgment that AI is here; it's a reality. And with that acceptance comes another real important word: commitment.

Acceptance and commitment therapy is a whole thing worth exploring. With acceptance, with the acknowledgment that AI is here, it's likely not going away, despite my feelings and my grief around it. Making peace with that fact allows us to commit to doing our part to make sure that we're putting good things out into the world. We're able to do our part to ensure that it's wielded in a safe and responsible way, and that we can do our part to move towards betterment rather than shittiness.

Just to underscore this once again, getting to this place doesn't mean that you also aren't still pissed off, you also aren't worried, you also aren't anxious, you also aren't depressed. It's a real willingness to address this reality head-on and realize that we are in a place of agency and empowerment, and that we can move forward with resolve and try to make the world a better place.

In Summary

  • Grief is a powerful response to loss.

  • We grieve things other than death like the loss of relationships, identity, sense of purpose, health, money, home, dreams, expectations, community, and even ideas and ideals.

  • These shocks to our system can elicit a really powerful response that are captured in these five stages of grief: Denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance.

  • These stages are really just labels and are not a rigid or linear process; everyone ebbs and flows in and out of each of these stages at any given moment.

  • While these stages can be helpful descriptors, it's important to not fixate on them or feel like there's anything wrong with you if you're not further along in the stages of grief. We are complex emotional creatures and our emotional states change over time.

I hope you keep this in mind, and remember to go easy on yourself. Go easy on each other. Know that everyone's in their own place in feeling and processing this complex moment in time. And the best thing we could do is to be kind to one another and support one another.
